title: Lockheed's Backlog Hits $292B While Rheinmetall Misses Its Own Delivery Dates — the Order Book and the Factory Floor Diverge
subhead: Lockheed Martin posted a record $292 billion backlog and raised guidance for the second straight quarter, the same week Handelsblatt reported Rheinmetall's Skyranger slipping two to three years and the Bundeswehr substituting a rival's system. Demand is no longer the constraint in the Western defense industry — throughput is.

sections.heading: Lockheed Martin: $292 Billion on the Books, $52.5 Billion of It PAC-3
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $20.7 billion, up 11% from $18.6 billion a year earlier, with net earnings of $1.85 billion and diluted EPS of $7.97, according to the company's results as reported by Pulse2. Operating profit came in at $2.44 billion.

The headline number is the backlog: $292 billion, up 27% quarter over quarter. Roughly $52.5 billion of that is tied to a multiyear award for PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors. The Missiles and Fire Control segment alone carries about $142.5 billion in backlog — nearly half the company's total.

Segment performance tells the story of where demand sits. Missiles and Fire Control sales rose 24% to $4.50 billion, with about $480 million of the increase coming from integrated air and missile defense programs including PAC-3 and THAAD, and $330 million more from GMLRS and Precision Strike Missiles. Aeronautics grew 13% to $8.21 billion, driven by roughly $710 million in additional F-35 revenue. Space, at $3.49 billion, was lifted by Fleet Ballistic Missile and Next Generation Interceptor work.

Lockheed raised full-year guidance for the second consecutive quarter — revenue to roughly $80–82 billion, EPS to $30.35–30.75, and free cash flow to $7.8–8 billion from a prior $7.0–7.2 billion. The company also flagged that costs on the F-35 Lot 20 advance acquisition contract have exceeded existing contractual authorization and funding, and that additional US government authorization will be needed to avoid charges in future periods.
sections.whyItMatters: The mix is the message: growth is concentrated in munitions and missile defense, not aircraft. Interceptors are now the scarcest commodity in Western arsenals, and the PAC-3 multiyear is the clearest sign that the Pentagon is buying production capacity years out. But the F-35 Lot 20 funding gap shows even the largest prime can be squeezed by an under-funded contract vehicle.

sections.heading: Rheinmetall's Skyranger Slips Two to Three Years — and Berlin Buys the Rival's System
sections.body:
Handelsblatt reported that Rheinmetall's Skyranger anti-aircraft gun tank has slipped by two to three years, and that the Bundeswehr's response is to bridge the capability gap with 48 GARMR drone-defence systems from Diehl — a competitor. Ad Hoc News, which reviewed the reporting, notes the programme has not been cancelled and Diehl has not permanently displaced Rheinmetall, but the substitution is a procurement workaround with commercial consequences.

This is not a one-off. German media, including Stern and fr.de, have reported Bundeswehr expectations of Skyranger deliveries sliding by up to 16 months, with first serial vehicles not reaching the fleet until 2027. Earlier reporting cited potential penalties in the region of €25 million for delivery delays.

The same week brought the counter-signal. Reuters, citing Italian daily MF, reported that Italy's Leonardo and Rheinmetall, through their joint venture, secured two Italian Army contracts worth €3.7 billion ($4.16 billion) combined for A2CS fighting vehicles and main battle tanks. Both caveats matter: neither company has officially confirmed the award, and the figure covers the joint venture rather than Rheinmetall's own revenue line. UBS trimmed its Rheinmetall price target to €1,360 from €1,600 while keeping a buy rating.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest European illustration of the gap between order intake and deliverable output. A customer that substitutes a rival system does so on a schedule, and those schedules are now measured in years. For Rheinmetall the €3.7 billion Italian win and the Skyranger slippage are not contradictory data points — they are the same problem viewed from the sales side and the production side. The Q3 report on 5 November is the next hard checkpoint.

sections.heading: Telford: Large-Calibre Gun Barrel Production Returns to Britain After Two Decades
sections.body:
Rheinmetall officially opened its UK Gun Hall in Telford on 22 October 2026, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting present, according to Janes. The facility restores independent British production of large-calibre weapon systems after roughly twenty years during which the country relied on imports for tank barrels.

At full tilt the site can produce up to 245 barrels and more than 50 breech mechanisms a year, with over 100 skilled jobs created during ramp-up, per Business Matters and the Shropshire Star. Breech mechanisms have been made there since May 2026 and barrels since June 2026. The plant processes steel from Sheffield Forgemasters, anchoring the supply chain domestically, and is set up for 120mm and 155mm systems including Challenger 3 and future artillery platforms. Rheinmetall built out the previously empty hall in eight months and says it has invested more than £200 million in Britain over five years. The facility sits under UK-German cooperation in the Trinity House agreement.

Janes and Business Matters both frame the opening as a supply-chain event rather than an order event. The capacity figures describe what the plant could make, not what is contracted.
sections.whyItMatters: Barrels and breech mechanisms were among the quietest bottlenecks in European rearmament — a single-source dependency that constrained artillery and tank output across multiple programmes. Bringing that capacity onshore compresses lead times for Challenger 3 and future artillery. It also illustrates a template: rather than waiting for a multinational framework, a prime built a hall in eight months and started cutting steel.

sections.heading: Raytheon Wins $8 Billion Sole-Source Deal to Rebuild Nuclear Command Links
sections.body:
The US Air Force awarded Raytheon an IDIQ contract with an $8 billion maximum ceiling for developmental modernization, production restart services, and technical studies on the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center's Strategic Communications Terminals, Military & Aerospace Electronics reports. The award was made sole-source by the Nuclear Weapons Center at Hanscom Air Force Base under contract FA2293-27-D-B001, with just $800,000 obligated at award from fiscal 2026 RDT&E funds. Work runs to 12 October 2036 at Marlborough, Massachusetts and Largo, Florida.

These terminals underpin nuclear command, control and communications — the link between national command authorities and strategic forces, including transmission of Emergency Action Messages. Raytheon's earlier Minuteman Minimum Essential Emergency Communications Network Program Upgrade incorporated the eXtended Data Rate waveform, which the company reported moved data more than five times faster than prior EHF satellite systems and enabled protected voice, data and video with cryptographic protection.

The announcement does not specify which terminal models are covered or whether the work touches AEHF-compatible terminals or other strategic communications systems. The $8 billion is a ceiling, not obligated funding — future work depends on task orders issued under the vehicle.
sections.whyItMatters: The words 'production restart' in a nuclear C3 contract are the tell. It implies the industrial base that built these terminals has atrophied enough that restarting lines is itself a funded task line. As the US modernizes Minuteman III's replacement and the broader NC3 architecture, the communications layer is the part that cannot be surged late.

sections.heading: Korean Peninsula: Cheap Long-Range Strike Drones Enter a Balance Built on Missiles and Nuclear Weapons
sections.body:
Both Koreas are developing low-cost long-range attack drones, with some systems slated to be operational in the near term, according to a Diplomat analysis. The piece, drawing on reporting from CSIS's Beyond Parallel, 38 North, Korea Herald and JoongAng, describes both sides converging on a deep-strike contest modeled on Ukraine and the Middle East.

North Korea in 2024 ordered officials to 'establish a mass-production system and begin full-scale operation' of suicide attack drones. Thousands of North Korean laborers, and possibly engineers, have reportedly been sent to the Yelabuga factory in Russia producing copies of Iran's Shahed one-way attack drone. Pyongyang has also unveiled a HALE reconnaissance drone and a MALE multi-role drone capable of firing a missile, though in limited numbers.

South Korea's Agency for Defense Development is developing the KUS-LM, dubbed 'K-LUCAS', with range and payload figures reported as comparable to the American LUCAS one-way attack drone, planned for deployment before 2030; trials have begun on land and sea. The Air Force has four Global Hawks delivered by 2020, and the domestic KUS-FS MALE drone is expected in service in 2027.

Separately, the New York Times reported on 23 October that a rare escalation this month exposed the increasingly lethal arsenals both Koreas are building, with the North emboldened by its Russia alliance. President Lee Jae Myung oversaw South Korea's first test-firing of a domestically developed hypersonic missile on 8 October, per Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The Diplomat's core judgment is that North Korea's ability to disperse, conceal and employ drones, missiles and nuclear weapons is outpacing South Korea's capacity to find and destroy them. That has a direct procurement consequence: South Korea's timeline for taking wartime operational control from the US rests on qualitative conditions, and cheap attack drones widen the ISR and counter-UAV gap Seoul must close first.

sections.heading: Aselsan Signs a $442.5 Million Radar and Counter-UAV Export Package
sections.body:
Aselsan announced on 23 October an international export contract worth $442.5 million covering radar systems, counter-UAV solutions and command-and-control systems for an undisclosed foreign client, per ShiftDelete. Delivery timelines and equipment quantities were not disclosed, and the company gave no breakdown of how the value splits across the three technology lines.

The package structure is notable rather than the headline figure: sensor, effector and the C2 layer that fuses them, sold as one integrated air-defence modernization rather than as standalone hardware. That is the model Aselsan has been pushing with its KORKUT 35mm self-propelled gun system, which the company says is deployed in nine countries and has engaged hundreds of drones — a cost-per-intercept argument aimed squarely at the cheap-drone problem.

The Financial Times reported Turkey marketing a roughly $10,000-per-engagement drone defence, with Aselsan positioning gun-based systems against low-cost kamikaze UAVs where missile interceptors are economically unsustainable. Aselsan has separately disclosed the GÖKALP E1 intercepting a target drone after AURA radar detection and DRONEDEF cueing in an October demonstration, per Quwa.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's export pitch has shifted from platform sales to layered air-defence packages priced against a drone threat that most buyers now consider permanent. Undisclosed customers are the norm in this market, but the recurring pattern is Gulf, Southeast Asian and Central Asian buyers seeking systems that do not carry US end-use restrictions. That is a durable commercial advantage for Ankara.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Is Expanding Its Solid-Fuel Missile Plant — Right as Washington Negotiates Enrichment
sections.body:
Satellite imagery analyzed by the Foreign Policy Research Institute shows Saudi Arabia expanding its solid-propellant missile production plant at al-Duwadimi, according to Reuters and the FPRI analysis by Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman. Two new buildings are under construction: one assessed as a casting facility for solid-propellant rocket motors with 5–6 metre pits and blast walls, the other a probable storage site for ammonium perchlorate or finished missile components. Ground clearing began in April 2025, concrete footings were poured in autumn 2025, and the work was near completion by mid-September 2026.

Casting pit diameter is the hard constraint on missile diameter, so larger pits imply larger motors — and therefore greater range or heavier payload. Saudi Arabia has produced ballistic missiles at al-Duwadimi since late 2021 with Chinese assistance, having long imported DF-3s; FPRI notes that DF-15A wreckage appearing in Yemen in September was the first indication Riyadh had used any of the missiles it spent decades importing from China.

The timing is the pointed part. The expansion is proceeding while Washington and Riyadh negotiate an agreement that may permit domestic uranium enrichment — a deal FPRI has separately argued abandons the 'gold standard' of no-enrichment, no-reprocessing.
sections.whyItMatters: Missile range and nuclear latency are two variables in the same equation, and Riyadh is expanding both at once. A larger-diameter solid motor is the delivery vehicle half of a deterrent; enrichment is the other. Washington is negotiating the second while commercial imagery tracks the first, and neither conversation is being held in public.

bottomLine: Demand is not the binding constraint in Western defense manufacturing. Lockheed's $292 billion backlog and Rheinmetall's Italian €3.7 billion win both landed the same week that Handelsblatt reported Skyranger slipping two to three years and the Bundeswehr substituting Diehl's GARMR system, and that Raytheon picked up an $8 billion nuclear communications contract whose scope includes 'production restart' services. The industry's problem has moved from the order book to the factory floor — and to the funding lines behind it, as Lockheed's unbudgeted F-35 Lot 20 costs show. Meanwhile the demand side is diversifying away from the old architecture: Aselsan is selling integrated sensor-shooter air-defence packages at $442.5 million a tranche, Seoul and Pyongyang are both buying into cheap long-range strike drones before 2030, and Riyadh is building casting pits large enough for bigger solid motors while negotiating enrichment with Washington.
sources: Pulse2, Military & Aerospace Electronics, Ad Hoc News, Reuters, Janes, Business Matters, Shropshire Star, The Diplomat, 38 North, CSIS Beyond Parallel, Korea Herald, JoongAng, New York Times, ShiftDelete, Financial Times, Quwa, Foreign Policy Research Institute, Eurasia Review, UBS
